Part 1

Runoff and the hydrograph

Definitions, where runoff comes from, and how a hydrograph records it

Definitions to remember

Key idea

Runoff is the part of precipitation, snowmelt or irrigation water that ends up in streams, drains or the soil profile instead of evaporating or being stored.

  • Runoff: precipitation, snowmelt or irrigation water that appears in uncontrolled surface streams, rivers, drains, or within the soil profile
  • Streamflow: volume of water moving past a point over a fixed time, often in cubic feet per second (ft³/s)
  • Discharge: outflow of water from a pipe or drainage basin through a channel into a stream, river, lake or ocean
  • Hydrograph: a graph of stage, flow, velocity or other water properties over time
  • Peak flow: the maximum discharge during the runoff from a storm
  • Baseflow: streamflow that is not runoff and instead comes from the ground

What is runoff?

Key idea

Precipitation generates runoff, and runoff generates streamflow.

  1. When infiltration capacity (Lecture 5e) is exceeded, excess precipitation becomes depression storage (Lecture 5c)
  2. Excess precipitation and depression storage eventually become runoff (overland flow)

Read the graph

The dashed curve is infiltration capacity. Rain below it infiltrates (gray); the first excess fills depression storage (white); the rest is overland flow (black).

Understanding the hydrograph

Key idea

A hydrograph is a continuous record of streamflow, discharge, river stage or well level. It shows a watershed’s non-linear response to rain.

Read the hydrograph

  • Rising limb: discharge climbs after rain starts
  • Peak flow rate: the highest discharge
  • Falling limb and recession: flow drains away
  • Basin lag: time from the center of rainfall to the peak
  • Baseflow: groundwater contribution under the storm flow

What shapes it?

Basin size, slope and shape, soil and bedrock, vegetation, land cover and soil moisture.

Types of hydrograph

Key idea

Hydrographs can cover a year, a season, a month or a single storm.

  • Annual: daily, weekly or 10-day mean flow over a year
  • Seasonal: discharge in a particular season, such as a monsoon or dry season
  • Monthly: daily mean flows over a month
  • Flood: streamflow from one storm over a catchment

Try it

The USGS Water Data site gives live hydrographs like this one for gauges near you, such as Johnson Creek in Gresham.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 What is the difference between baseflow and runoff on a storm hydrograph?

Runoff (storm flow) is the quick response to rain; baseflow is the steady contribution from groundwater that continues between storms.

Q2 On a storm hydrograph, what is the basin lag?

The time between the center of mass of the rainfall and the peak flow.

Part 2

What shapes the hydrograph

Physiographic factors (basin, infiltration, channel) and climatic factors

Basin shape and size

  1. Basin
  2. Infiltration
  3. Channel
  4. Climate
Key idea

Hydrograph factors are physiographic or climatic. First, the basin characteristics: shape and size.

(a) Shape

A radial basin drains faster than an elongated one, giving a sharper peak. A basin of divided subbasins can give a double peak.

(b) Size

In a larger watershed runoff takes longer to reach the outlet, so the peak is more gradual.

Slope, drainage density, valley and elevation

  1. Basin
  2. Infiltration
  3. Channel
  4. Climate
Key idea

Steeper basins and denser drainage networks move water to the outlet faster, so peaks come earlier and higher.

  • (c) Slope: the greater the slope, the faster overland flow reaches the outlet
  • (d) Drainage density: more channel length per area drains faster and forms peaks earlier
  • (e) Nature of the valley: runoff velocity is higher in a steeper valley
  • (f) Elevation: more rain falls on the windward side at higher elevations, which also adds to slope differences

Hydrograph and urbanization

  1. Basin
  2. Infiltration
  3. Channel
  4. Climate
Key idea

Development adds impervious surface and cuts infiltration, so urban watersheds are flashier: earlier, higher peaks.

Read the figure

Curve (a), a natural watershed, has a low, late peak. Curve (b) is partially developed. Curve (c), fully developed with storm drains, peaks sooner and much higher.

Storm sewers deliver water to the channel far faster than overland flow through soil and vegetation.

Infiltration characteristics

  1. Basin
  2. Infiltration
  3. Channel
  4. Climate
Key idea

Anything that lets water soak in or be stored lowers and delays the peak.

  • (a) Land use / land cover: development and vegetation type change soil and permeability
  • (b) Soil type and geology: directly control infiltration rate and permeability
  • (c) Lakes, swamps and other storage: reduce peak flow, and increase evaporation loss

Read the figures

A vegetated basin and a permeable soil both give a lower, later, broader peak.

Channel characteristics

  1. Basin
  2. Infiltration
  3. Channel
  4. Climate
Key idea

Channel shape, roughness and storage change how fast water travels downstream.

  • (a) Cross section: V-shaped channels give higher velocity, which can raise the peak
  • (b) Roughness: rough beds (boulders) create friction and slow flow; smooth beds (small pebbles) speed it up and raise the peak
  • (c) Storage capacity: channels that can hold more water during storms reduce the water that becomes runoff downstream

Climatic factors

  1. Basin
  2. Infiltration
  3. Channel
  4. Climate
Key idea

Storm amount, intensity, duration and movement drive the hydrograph, after initial losses and evaporation.

(1) Storm characteristics

  • Precipitation: how much water (mm)
  • Intensity: how fast (mm/h)
  • Duration: longer (h) means more water
  • Movement of the storm: where the water falls

(2) Initial loss: usually interception and storage. (3) Evaporation: from surfaces, depending on the atmosphere.

Read the graph

Same climate, different geology: the red stream is flashy, the blue one smooth.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q3 Two watersheds have the same area and rainfall. One is radial with steep slopes; the other is elongated and gentle. Which has the higher, earlier peak?

The radial, steep watershed: water from all parts reaches the outlet at about the same time, and steep slopes move it faster.

Q4 Why does urbanization make a hydrograph “flashier”?

Impervious surfaces stop infiltration and storm drains carry water quickly to the channel, so more runoff arrives sooner: an earlier, higher peak.

Q5 How does a large wetland upstream of a gauge change the hydrograph?

It stores water, so the peak is lower and later, and some water is lost to evaporation.

Part 3

Hydrographs across climates and watersheds

Climate regimes, river types, hydrograph components and sediment

Hydrograph by climate

Key idea

The shape of the annual hydrograph reflects the climate: when water arrives and when it is released.

  • Glacier melt: peak in late summer, when the ice melts
  • High summer evaporation: high flow in winter, lowest in summer (like panel D)
  • Tropical seasonal: peak in the wet season
  • Snowmelt: peak in late spring to early summer as the snowpack melts

Each panel (A–D) peaks in a different month: the timing is the fingerprint of the climate.

Seasonal variation in the hydrograph

Key idea

Hydrographs vary between dry and wet years, and with the type and timing of precipitation.

Read the left graph

A flood season stands out above the long-term mean annual discharge; the shaded area is the annual flood volume.

Read the right graph

Snow-dominated rivers peak sharply in May; high-elevation melt keeps flow high from June to August; rain-dominated rivers have peaks in spring and fall.

In the Pacific Northwest you can find all three.

Hydrograph and river regime

Key idea

A hydrograph tells you what type of stream you are looking at. USGS provides excellent hydrograph data.

  • Perennial (“typical”): constant streamflow all year; discharge is almost never zero
  • Ephemeral: dry streams that flow only after rainfall
  • Intermittent: stops flowing only in very dry periods, usually zero in summer

Components of a hydrograph

Key idea

A storm hydrograph is the sum of several flow paths that arrive at different times.

  • Runoff (overland flow): fast, makes the peak
  • Baseflow (groundwater flow): slow and steady
  • Direct precipitation on the channel: arrives first
  • Interflow (near-surface flow): in between

Read the figures

Left: quickflow rides on top of baseflow, with a rising limb, crest, falling limb and recession. Right: total streamflow split into each component.

Hydrographs within a watershed

Key idea

The hydrograph can be different at different points in the same watershed.

Read the figure

Gauges in small headwater streams show sharp, quick peaks. Downstream gauges show larger, later, smoother peaks as flow from many tributaries combines and is stored in the channel.

Runoff can carry a lot of sediment

Key idea

Runoff moves sediment in three steps: detachment, transport and deposition.

  1. Detachment: raindrops and flow loosen particles
  2. Transport: runoff carries them downslope
  3. Deposition: they settle where flow slows

Read the images

After Hurricane Irene passed over Florida (Oct. 1999), runoff left huge sediment plumes in coastal waters (left); by Dec. 2002 the water was clear (right). Credit: NASA Visible Earth.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q6 A river’s annual hydrograph peaks in May–June with low flow in late summer. Which climate type is that most like?

Snowmelt-dominated: the peak follows the spring and early summer melt of the snowpack.

Q7 A stream gauge shows zero discharge most of the year with brief spikes after storms. What type of stream is it?

Ephemeral.

Part 4

Runoff mechanisms

Horton overland flow, saturation-excess overland flow and subsurface flow

Mechanism 1: Horton overland flow

  1. Horton overland flow
  2. Saturation excess
  3. Subsurface flow
Key idea

Horton (infiltration-excess) overland flow happens when rainfall intensity exceeds infiltration capacity.

Robert E. Horton (1875–1945)

  • First to formalize infiltration theory
  • Runoff forms when rainfall intensity > infiltration capacity
  • Infiltration rates decline during storms
  • The water table does not need to reach the surface

Where?

Common on urban, impervious, hydrophobic or compacted soils. Rare on vegetated surfaces in humid regions.

The Horton overland flow model

  1. Horton overland flow
  2. Saturation excess
  3. Subsurface flow
Key idea

Horton’s equation (Lecture 5e) gives the infiltration capacity at time t. Rain above it becomes overland flow.

fp = fc + (f0 − fc) e−kt

  • fp: infiltration capacity
  • fc: equilibrium infiltration capacity
  • f0: initial infiltration capacity
  • k: constant depending on soil type
  • t: time from the beginning of rain

Assumptions

Freely drained soil; constant rainfall intensity.

Read the graph

fp (red) falls toward fc (dashed) while F, cumulative infiltration (orange), keeps rising.

Mechanism 2: saturation-excess overland flow

  1. Horton overland flow
  2. Saturation excess
  3. Subsurface flow
Key idea

Also called Dunne overland flow: the soil becomes saturated as the water table rises, so any more rain must run off.

It is unable to hold any more water, so additional rain runs off.

Where?

Mainly at the bottom of hillslopes and near stream banks.

Read the figures

(a) The water table is below the surface. (b) It rises to the surface near the stream. Soil water that moved downslope as throughflow seeps out again as return flow, adding to saturation overland flow.

Infiltration excess vs. saturation excess

  1. Horton overland flow
  2. Saturation excess
  3. Subsurface flow
Key idea

Both make overland flow, for different reasons: rain too fast, or soil too full.

Infiltration-excess (Horton)

Infiltration capacity is exceeded. The soil below may still be dry: water simply cannot enter fast enough.

Saturation-excess (Dunne)

The ground is saturated. Even gentle rain runs off because there is no room left.

Mechanism 3: throughflow, interflow and lateral flow

  1. Horton overland flow
  2. Saturation excess
  3. Subsurface flow
Key idea

Water can also move sideways below the surface: subsurface storm flow.

  • Lateral movement in the unsaturated (vadose) zone, through the soil profile
  • Also called throughflow, interflow or subsurface storm flow
  • Happens when infiltrating water hits a less permeable layer, such as rock
  • The permeability difference must be large enough; otherwise the water keeps infiltrating downward

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q8 A parking lot floods in a short, intense thunderstorm while a nearby forest does not. Which runoff mechanism is that?

Horton (infiltration-excess) overland flow: rainfall intensity exceeds the very low infiltration capacity of the pavement.

Q9 After a week of steady rain, a valley floor near a stream produces runoff even in light drizzle. Which mechanism, and why there?

Saturation-excess (Dunne) overland flow. The water table has risen to the surface at the bottom of the slope near the stream.

Q10 What condition is needed for interflow to occur?

A less permeable layer below the soil, with a large enough permeability contrast to turn infiltrating water sideways.

Part 5

Floods and how we manage them

When runoff exceeds what rivers and drains can carry

Too much runoff leads to flooding

Key idea

When excess runoff exceeds the carrying capacity of rivers, streams and storage systems, flooding occurs.

heavy rain → impervious surfaces → less infiltration → more runoff → flood

Floods happen in urban and rural areas. Land use / land cover and ground permeability drive their intensity, along with how much rain falls.

  • Urban flooding: storm water inflow exceeds the capacity of the urban drainage system to infiltrate or carry it away
  • Rural flooding: heavy rain over flat land, rivers breaching embankments, raised groundwater, tidal surges

Drivers of flooding

Key idea

Extreme precipitation such as atmospheric rivers, and sea level rise, are major flood drivers, made worse by impervious surfaces.

Read the figure (left)

  • Natural ground cover: 10% runoff, 50% infiltration
  • 10–20% impervious: 20% runoff
  • 35–50% impervious: 30% runoff
  • 75–100% impervious: 55% runoff, only 15% infiltration

As cities pave over the land, more of every storm becomes runoff.

Flood prevention and adaptation strategies

Key idea

We can manage floods with gray infrastructure, green infrastructure, or both.

Gray infrastructure

Built structures: dams, seawalls, roads, pipes and water treatment plants.

Green infrastructure

Natural systems such as forests, floodplains, wetlands and soils that also provide other benefits for human well-being, like flood protection and climate regulation.

Runoff recap

Key idea

Runoff (streamflow generation) has three main mechanisms: Horton overland flow, interflow and saturation-excess overland flow.

Fates of precipitation

  1. Canopy interception → throughfall, stemflow or evaporation
  2. Direct precipitation → streamflow or surface water storage
  3. Infiltration → interflow, soil moisture storage or groundwater recharge
  4. Overland flow → Horton or saturation-excess overland flow

Streamflow-generation mechanisms

a. Horton overland flow; b. interflow (subsurface); c. saturation-excess overland flow

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q11 Using the impervious-surface figure, how much more of a storm becomes runoff in a 75–100% impervious area than under natural cover?

About 55% vs. 10%: more than five times as much runoff.

Q12 Name one gray and one green approach to reducing urban flood peaks.

Gray: a storm sewer, detention pipe or dam. Green: a wetland, floodplain, rain garden, green roof or permeable pavement.
